Apple and OpenEvidence launched a study app that lets iPhone users ask an AI health questions and grade every answer.
Apple wants up to 200,000 US participants aged 21 and over, for more than 12 months.
Users can share sleep, heart rate and lab results, and Apple says the data will not train AI models.

threads_text: Apple now wants up to 200,000 iPhone users to ask an AI their health questions and grade every answer, in a year long study built with OpenEvidence. It reads like Apple testing the waters before an AI health coach. Would you share your lab results with it?

paragraphs.text: Apple and OpenEvidence launched a study app on November 15, 2026 that lets iPhone users in the United States ask an AI health questions and grade the answers, STAT reported. Apple is seeking up to 200,000 participants and plans to run the study for more than 12 months, according to Startup Fortune and Gagadget.

STAT described the app as experimental and AI powered, and referred to the effort as the Apple Health AI Usage Study. It was developed with OpenEvidence, a medical evidence search engine that is popular with clinicians, and uses some of that company's technology.

Participants ask health questions in the app, such as how to improve sleep or heart health, STAT reported. They then rate each answer on accuracy, detail and relevance and complete a monthly survey about how they used the information, according to Startup Fortune.

Users can choose to share data from Apple's Health app, including resting heart rate, activity, sleep and lab results, to get answers tailored to them. Apple also suggests the app can help people prepare for doctor's appointments, and Gagadget reported that it points users to a medical professional when a question suggests a possibly serious problem.

Answers draw on clinical literature, including papers from the New England Journal of Medicine, JAMA and Nature, according to Startup Fortune and Gagadget. Startup Fortune added that the app has guardrails for concerning questions and is not designed to diagnose or treat conditions.

Startup Fortune reported that participants must live in the United States, be 21 or older, run iOS 26 or later and have Apple Intelligence turned on. Gagadget noted that outlets give different device requirements, so the App Store listing is the place to check. Users in the United Kingdom cannot take part.

Apple says study data is anonymized on the iPhone before it is sent to a secure third party cloud provider and that the data will not be used to train AI models. Apple also says OpenEvidence deletes questions and answers after 24 hours. Gagadget pointed out that these are the company's own claims and have not been independently audited.

Sumbul Desai, Apple's vice president of health and fitness, said a dedicated research study is the most careful way to learn how people use AI for health questions, according to Startup Fortune. Gagadget reported that she framed the results as a way for Apple to understand how people use medical AI tools.

OpenEvidence was valued at $12 billion in a funding round in January 2026 and is used by more than 40 percent of US physicians, Startup Fortune reported, citing MLQ.ai. STAT noted that Apple has reportedly been working on an AI health coach and that the study may shape future Apple products.

The setup suggests Apple wants evidence before it puts AI health answers in front of a wide audience. Asking users to grade every answer gives the company a large, structured record of where an AI helps and where it confuses people, which is the kind of data a cautious health product would need.
Apple has not said whether AI answers will reach the Health app or Siri, and it has not published any results. With a study planned to run more than a year, the findings are unlikely to arrive soon.
Watch whether Apple publishes the study's findings and whether a version of these health answers appears in the Health app or Siri in a future iOS release.
